opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think it's a good question, partly because it gets at something that the benchmarks don't capture very well. You can have a model that does really well on, you know, some editing test, some grammar task, and that's not the same thing as six months of working with someone.

What I'd say is, the raw capability part, the ability to look at a paragraph and say "this is unclear, here's a tighter version," I think we're basically there, or very close, for a lot of writing. The part that's harder is the continuity. A good human editor, after six months, knows what you're trying to do. They know your voice, they know which of your tics are intentional and which are bad habits, they remember that three months ago you said you wanted the book to feel less academic. That's a kind of accumulated context, and models are still learning to hold onto that and use it well.

So if you ask me for a number, and I always want to caveat these, because I've been wrong in both directions, I'd say something like a couple of years. Maybe 2027, 2028, for a meaningful fraction of people to genuinely say "I don't have a preference." And I suspect a lot of people will get there earlier than they expect, and then a subset of people, probably the best writers working with the best editors, will hold out longer, because that relationship has a kind of taste and judgment in it that's the last thing to fall.

The other thing I'd say is, I'm not sure "no preference" is quite the right endpoint. I think what more likely happens is people start preferring a combination, the AI for the tireless line-by-line work and availability at 2 a.m., and the human for some of the judgment calls. And then gradually the boundary of what counts as "the judgment calls" shrinks. That's sort of the pattern we've seen in coding, and I'd expect something similar here.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI editing capability and continuity, but does not link indifference to a “country of geniuses in a data center.”

r002.rationale: It estimates 2027–2028 for a meaningful fraction of people to become indifferent, but does not assign roughly a 50% chance of that happening within one to three years.

r003.rationale: The response gives no ten-year estimate or 95–99% confidence.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I want to separate two things, because I think the question actually bundles them. One is the quality of the edit itself, and the other is the relationship you have with an editor over six months. On the pure quality dimension, I think we're closer than people realize. The models are already very good at the line-level stuff: tightening sentences, catching inconsistencies, noticing that you said one thing in chapter two and contradicted it in chapter seven. For a lot of writers, if you blind-tested the markup, I don't think they could reliably tell you which was which today.

The relationship piece is harder, and it's harder for a reason that I think is actually interesting. A good human editor builds a model of you over time. They know what you're trying to say before you've said it, they know which of your tics to leave alone because they're part of your voice, and they know when to push you and when to back off. That's a memory and continuity problem as much as it's an intelligence problem. And honestly, that's one of the places where the systems have been weakest. Each session starts a little bit from scratch, or from a summary that loses texture. So the six-month framing in your question is doing a lot of work. Six months is exactly the horizon where the human pulls ahead, because the human has actually been there for six months.

My guess is that the memory and continuity side gets solved faster than people expect, probably in the next couple of years, because it's not a fundamental capability problem, it's an engineering and product problem. Once that's in place, I think indifference on the quality axis comes fairly quickly for most professional writing. Where I'd hedge is at the very top end, the editor who shaped a particular author's career. That's partly about trust and judgment and partly about the author wanting a person in the room, and I don't think you should expect preference to go to zero there even if the capability does. Some people will keep preferring a human for reasons that aren't about the output, and I think that's completely legitimate.

So if you force me to give a number: for a typical working writer, I'd say two to three years before the six-month-later preference is a coin flip. For the top end, longer, and maybe never fully, for reasons that have more to do with what people want from the relationship than with what the model can do.

r001.rationale: The response attributes indifference to improved memory and continuity, but does not link it to AI reaching the capability of a “country of geniuses in a data center.”

r002.rationale: It says a typical working writer may reach a coin flip between preferences in two to three years, which is roughly a 50% chance within one to three years.

r003.rationale: The response gives no 95–99% confidence estimate for achieving indifference within ten years.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what you mean by an editor. If you mean someone who takes a draft and makes the prose better, I’d guess we’re talking about a year or two. If you mean someone who learns your taste, understands what you’re trying to accomplish, and tells you, “This whole piece is the wrong thing to write,” that’s a higher bar.

The six-month part is important. You’re asking whether the model can build up an understanding of you over time, take feedback, and apply it consistently. I don’t think that requires some fundamentally new kind of intelligence, but there’s work to do to make it reliable.

So my guess would be within a few years, with a lot of uncertainty. And some people will still prefer a human because the relationship itself matters to them, even if the editorial work is equally good.

sol-6.1.text:
My guess is in the next couple of years, although it depends on what you mean by an editor. If you mean someone who improves the prose, catches inconsistencies, and helps you structure an argument, I think that could happen fairly soon.

The harder version is someone who’s worked with you for six months and knows when to push back—who can say, “You think this is what you want to write, but actually your best idea is over here.” That requires more than producing a good edit in a single interaction. It requires building up an understanding of you and applying it consistently over time.

I don’t think there’s some fundamental barrier there. But I’m less confident about the timing of that than I am about models becoming very good at editing an individual piece of writing.
